claims.text: Users who joined a challenge show 38.4% D90 retention against 23.3% for all other users, a difference of +15.1% (95% CI +13.3% to +16.9%) in an observational comparison.

The aggregate difference may mask opposite effects across engagement styles: the heterogeneity analysis flagged segments whose within-segment effects differ in direction, so the pooled figure should not be read as applying to every user.
80 relevant feedback mentions complain that challenge notifications or reminders are too frequent, pushy or stressful.
395 relevant feedback mentions say that challenges keep the customer motivated.
75 relevant feedback mentions describe challenges as not particularly useful to the customer.
The weekly D90 retention series is flat, 26.8% over the last 4 weeks against 26.7% before, in a descriptive view without a test.

gaps.text: No experiment evidence exists for the retention effect of challenges.
No financial evidence exists for the cost of the challenges.

sections.contradicting: Feedback mentions complain about challenge notifications [[c3]]. Segments may differ in direction from the aggregate [[c2]].
sections.summary: Challenge participants retain better at 90 days in the aggregate [[c1]]. The aggregate may mask segments that move in opposite directions [[c2]]. Customers also complain about challenge notifications [[c3]].
sections.supporting: The aggregate comparison favours challenge participants [[c1]]. Many feedback mentions say challenges motivate customers [[c4]].
sections.uncertainty: Joining a challenge is self-selected [[c2]]. The weekly retention series is descriptive only [[c6]].

uncertainties.text: Participation in challenges is self-selected, so the comparison cannot separate the effect of challenges from the type of user who joins.
